chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, safety and measuring

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The manufacturing technician job and the CPT 4.0
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what a production technician does and which credential shows employers you are ready.
This lesson builds toward: Using the MSSC CPT 4.0 page and local training options, you will write a dated plan to prepare for the CPT 4.0 and a first production job, that names the four required modules, a test date to confirm, and an honest résumé line.
A production technician helps make products safely and correctly. On a normal shift you may set up or run a machine, assemble parts, check parts with measuring tools, record numbers on a sheet or screen, keep your area clean, and report problems with machines or parts.
Many employers look for the Certified Production Technician (CPT 4.0) from the Manufacturing Skill Standards Council (MSSC). It has five assessments: Safety; Quality Practices & Measurement; Manufacturing Process & Production; Maintenance Awareness; and Green Production. You earn a certificate for each one you pass. The first four together earn the full CPT 4.0. Green Production is optional.
MSSC says the tests are multiple choice and can be given online or on paper. Training is offered through community colleges, workforce programs and some high schools. MSSC also has a hands-on option called CPT+ with Skill Boss. Check msscusa.org for current fees, testing sites and requirements; this course does not grant the credential.
Other paths into the work: registered apprenticeships, where you earn while you learn (search apprenticeship.gov), and jobs where the employer trains you. Veterans who did maintenance or supply work in the military often have skills that carry over.
Words to know:
- Production technician: a worker who runs, sets up, checks and cares for equipment that makes products.
- MSSC: the Manufacturing Skill Standards Council, the group that gives the CPT assessments and credentials.
- Assessment: a test that shows whether you know the material.
- Module: one topic area of the CPT, with its own assessment and certificate.
- Registered apprenticeship: a paid job with training and a mentor, recognized by the U.S. Department of Labor or a state.
Official sources:
- MSSC: Certified Production Technician (CPT 4.0)
- MSSC: CPT 4.0 modules and courses
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Finder (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: On paper, write the four CPT 4.0 modules you need for the full certification. Next to each, write one thing you already know about it and one question you have. Then open msscusa.org and write where you would look for a testing site.
You can now explain what a production technician does and name the four CPT 4.0 modules you need for the full credential.

check.q: How many CPT 4.0 modules must you pass for the full certification?
check.why: MSSC says candidates must earn the first four certificates for the full CPT 4.0; Green Production is optional.
MSSC gives the assessments and issues the credentials; this course only prepares you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Machine safety: guards, PPE and lockout/tagout
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the hazards on a machine and choose the right protection.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description or picture of a machine and a task, you will identify the hazards and choose the right protection, including lockout/tagout, naming at least 3 hazards and the correct protection for each.
OSHA says any machine part, function or process that may cause injury must be safeguarded. Its machine rule names hazards such as the point of operation (where the machine cuts, presses or shapes), ingoing nip points (where two parts roll together and can pull you in), rotating parts, and flying chips and sparks. Injuries can include crushing, amputation, burns and blindness.
Your protection, from strongest to weakest: guards that keep your body out of the danger zone (never remove or bypass one), safe procedures, and personal protective equipment (PPE) such as safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves where allowed and steel-toe shoes. Keep loose clothing, long hair and jewelry away from moving parts; gloves can be caught in rotating parts, so follow the rule for each machine.
Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is OSHA's rule 29 CFR 1910.147. When a machine is serviced or a jam is cleared, its energy (electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical or thermal) must be shut off and locked so it cannot start. Only trained, authorized employees apply locks. Everyone else is told never to remove a lock or restart locked equipment.
Federal child labor rules bar workers under 18 from many power-driven machines, such as metal forming, punching and shearing machines, power saws and forklifts. Check the Department of Labor page if you are under 18.
Step by step:
- Prepare: know every energy source of the machine.
- Tell the affected workers the machine is being shut down.
- Shut the machine down the normal way.
- Isolate the energy: switch off, close valves, disconnect.
- Put on your own lock and tag.
- Release or block stored energy (springs, air, pressure, heat).
- Verify: try to start it, then return the controls to off.
Words to know:
- Point of operation: the place where the machine cuts, bends, presses or shapes the material.
- Nip point: where two moving parts come together and can pull in fingers, hair or clothing.
- Guard: a barrier that keeps your body away from moving parts.
- PPE: personal protective equipment, like safety glasses, ear plugs and safety shoes.
- Lockout/tagout (LOTO): shutting off a machine's energy and putting on a lock and tag so it cannot start while someone works on it.
- Stored energy: energy left in a machine after it is switched off, such as a spring, air pressure or heat.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Machine Guarding
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212: General requirements for all machines (guarding)
- OSHA: Control of Hazardous Energy (Lockout/Tagout)
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147: The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
- U.S. Department of Labor: Jobs that are off-limits to workers under 18
Try it now: Pick a machine you know or can watch in a video: a drill press, a paper shredder or a conveyor. List at least three hazards (point of operation, nip points, rotating parts, flying chips) and the protection for each. Then read this practice case: a part is jammed in a press. Write what must happen before anyone reaches in.
You can now identify the hazards on a machine and choose guards, PPE or lockout/tagout to protect yourself and others.

check.q: A guard slows you down, and a coworker says to take it off. What do you do?
options: Take it off when the supervisor is away
Bend it out of the way
Remove it for one shift only
Keep it on and report the problem to the supervisor
check.why: Guards keep your body out of the danger zone and must never be removed or bypassed.

check.q: A machine must be serviced. What step comes right after you put on your lock and tag?
options: Release or block stored energy, then verify it will not start
Take the lock off to test it
check.why: After locking, you release stored energy and verify the machine cannot start.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Measuring parts and reading a tolerance
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Measure a part and decide whether it is within tolerance.
This lesson builds toward: Given a ruler or caliper reading and a part tolerance, you will measure a part and decide if it is within tolerance, getting at least 4 of 5 practice decisions right.
Every part has a target size on its drawing, called the nominal size, and a tolerance: how far it may be from the target and still be good. For example, 1.250 ± 0.005 inch means any size from 1.245 to 1.255 inches is good. Anything smaller or bigger is out of tolerance.
Common tools: a tape measure or steel rule for rough sizes; a caliper for outside, inside and depth sizes, often to a thousandth of an inch (0.001) or a hundredth of a millimeter (0.01); and a micrometer for even finer outside sizes. Many shops use digital calipers.
Good habits: clean the part and the tool, zero the caliper with the jaws closed, hold the jaws square to the part without squeezing, read the number straight on, and write it down right away. Measure more than once if you are unsure. Learn to use precision tools with an instructor, who will also teach reading dial and vernier scales.
Step by step:
- Read the drawing: nominal size and tolerance.
- Work out the limits: nominal minus and plus the tolerance.
- Clean the part and the tool; zero the caliper.
- Measure square, without squeezing; read the number.
- Write it down. Inside the limits = good; outside = out of tolerance.
Words to know:
- Nominal size: the target size shown on the drawing.
- Tolerance: how much a size may vary from the target and still be good.
- Caliper: a tool with sliding jaws that measures outside, inside and depth sizes.
- Micrometer: a screw-type tool that measures outside sizes very precisely.
- Zero: setting the tool to read 0 with the jaws closed, so readings start from the right point.
Official sources:
- MSSC: CPT 4.0 modules and courses
Try it now: Practice only, made-up numbers. A part is 2.000 ± 0.010 inch. Work out the limits, then decide good or out of tolerance for: 1.995, 2.012, 1.989, 2.010, 2.004. Next, measure three items at home with a ruler (a book, a phone, a spoon) twice each and write both readings.
You can now work out the limits of a tolerance, measure a part carefully and decide if it is good or out of tolerance.

check.q: A part is 0.500 ± 0.002 inch. Which range is good?
check.why: Subtract and add 0.002 to 0.500: the good range is 0.498 to 0.502.

check.q: What do you do with a digital caliper before measuring?
options: Measure the part while it is dirty
Close the jaws and zero it
check.why: Zeroing with the jaws closed makes every reading start from the right point.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Quality, production and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Quality checks and finding the root cause
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record defects and find a likely root cause with the 5 Whys.
This lesson builds toward: Given a quality problem on a production line, you will record the defects and find a likely root cause with the 5 Whys, separating the bad parts and reaching a cause that can be fixed.
Quality means every part meets its specification, the written requirements for size, look and function. A part that does not is a defect, or nonconforming part. Your job is to catch defects early, keep them away from good parts and report them.
Use a check sheet: a simple table where you make a tally mark each time you see a type of defect, such as scratch, wrong size or missing hole. After a shift the tallies show which problem happens most. Put bad parts in a marked reject bin or tag them so nobody ships them by mistake.
To fix a problem for good, find its root cause, not just the symptom. The 5 Whys is simple: state the problem, ask "Why?", then ask "Why?" about that answer, about five times, until you reach a cause you can fix. Many plants then use Plan-Do-Check-Act: plan a fix, try it, check the results, and make it the standard if it works.
Step by step:
- Check parts against the specification.
- Tally each defect type on a check sheet.
- Tag bad parts or put them in the reject bin; report them.
- Ask "Why?" about five times to reach a root cause.
- Suggest a fix; check that the defects drop.
Words to know:
- Specification: the written requirements a part must meet.
- Defect: a part or product that does not meet the specification; also called nonconforming.
- Check sheet: a table for tallying how often each type of defect happens.
- Root cause: the real reason a problem happens; fixing it stops the problem coming back.
- 5 Whys: asking "Why?" again and again to move from a symptom to its root cause.
- Plan-Do-Check-Act: a four-step cycle for testing a fix and making it standard.
Official sources:
- MSSC: CPT 4.0 modules and courses
Try it now: Practice case: holes drilled in brackets are in the wrong place on about one part in ten. Make a check sheet with three defect types and fill it with made-up tallies. Then write a 5 Whys chain (for example: the fixture moves, because a clamp is loose, because ...) and end with a fix you could suggest to your supervisor.
You can now record defects on a check sheet, separate bad parts, and use the 5 Whys to find a root cause.

check.q: You find five scratched parts in a bin of good parts. What do you do first?
options: Separate and tag them, then report it
Throw them away and say nothing
check.why: Bad parts are kept away from good ones and reported so the cause can be found.

check.q: What is the goal of the 5 Whys?
options: To find a root cause you can fix
check.why: The 5 Whys moves from a symptom to the root cause, so the fix lasts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Lean production, 5S and daily machine care
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Apply 5S and a daily operator check to a work area.
This lesson builds toward: Given a work area and a machine, you will apply 5S and a daily operator check to the area, listing an action for each of the 5 S's and at least 5 daily check items.
Lean production means making what the customer needs with less waste. Waste includes waiting, making too much, extra moving, extra handling, too much stock, defects and steps that add no value. Spotting waste and suggesting small improvements is part of a technician's job.
5S keeps a work area safe and efficient. Sort: remove what you do not need. Set in order: a marked place for every tool. Shine: clean the area and the machine, which also shows leaks and damage. Standardize: write down how the area should look. Sustain: keep doing it every shift.
Maintenance awareness starts with daily operator care. Before and during your shift, look for leaks, loose bolts, worn belts, low oil or coolant, strange noises, heat, vibration and damaged guards or cords. Follow the machine's checklist. Report what you find; only trained, authorized people repair machines, and repairs need lockout/tagout.
Preventive maintenance is planned care, such as oiling and changing filters on a schedule, so machines break down less. Your notes on the checklist help the maintenance team catch problems early.
Step by step:
- Sort: remove what you do not need.
- Set in order: a marked place for every tool.
- Shine: clean, and look for leaks and damage as you clean.
- Standardize: write or post how the area should look.
- Sustain: do it every shift.
- Daily check: leaks, noise, heat, vibration, belts, fluids, guards; report problems.
Words to know:
- Lean: a way of working that removes waste so value flows to the customer.
- Waste: anything that adds time or cost but no value, like waiting or extra moving.
- 5S: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain: a method for an orderly work area.
- Preventive maintenance: planned care on a schedule so machines break down less.
- Vibration: shaking that can be a sign of a loose or worn part.
Official sources:
- MSSC: CPT 4.0 modules and courses
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147: The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
Try it now: Pick one work area you can see now: a kitchen counter, a garage shelf or a desk. Write one action for each of the 5 S's. Then write a daily check list of at least five items for a machine you know (a car, a bike, a lawn mower or a washing machine) and what you would report.
You can now spot waste, use 5S on a work area and do a daily operator check, reporting problems instead of fixing them yourself.

check.q: Which 5S step means "a marked place for every tool"?
check.why: Set in order gives every tool a marked place so it is easy to find and return.

check.q: During your daily check you hear a new grinding noise. What do you do?
options: Write it on the checklist and report it
check.why: Operators report unusual noise; trained, authorized people repair it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your plan: CPT 4.0 prep and your first production job
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a dated plan to prepare for the CPT 4.0 and apply for production jobs.
This lesson builds toward: Using the MSSC CPT 4.0 page and local training options, you will write a dated plan to prepare for the CPT 4.0 and a first production job, that names the four required modules, a test date to confirm, and an honest résumé line.
Start with the official page. On msscusa.org, check the current modules, how testing is given, the fees and where to test. Many community colleges and workforce centers (often called American Job Centers) run CPT training and may help pay for it. Ask whether the program includes hands-on practice with real tools and machines.
Plan one module at a time. Safety is a good first module. For each, set study weeks, a practice method (notes, flash cards, the practice in this course) and a target test date that you confirm with the testing site.
Apply while you study. Look for production associate, machine operator, assembler and manufacturing technician jobs, and search apprenticeship.gov for registered apprenticeships. Some employers hire people with a record; workforce and re-entry programs can point you to them.
On your résumé, be honest. Write "Completed Manufacturing Technician Basics (Koach Learn), 2026" and list the CPT modules only after you pass them. In interviews, talk about safety first, measuring carefully, catching bad parts and keeping your area in order.
Step by step:
- Read the CPT 4.0 page on msscusa.org; note the four required modules.
- Find one local training program or testing site and what it offers.
- Set study weeks and a target date for each module; confirm dates with the site.
- List three job titles and three employers or apprenticeships to apply to.
- Write an honest résumé line and a 30-second answer: "Why manufacturing?"
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a public workforce office that helps people find jobs and training.
- Production associate: a common entry-level job title on a factory floor.
- Testing site: a school or center approved to give the assessment.
Official sources:
- MSSC: Certified Production Technician (CPT 4.0)
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Finder (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: Write your plan on one page: the four modules with a study start week and target test date for each, one program or testing site to contact, three jobs or apprenticeships to apply to, and your honest résumé line. Read your 30-second "Why manufacturing?" answer out loud.
You can now write a dated plan to prepare for the CPT 4.0 and a first production job, and describe your training honestly.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Hazard-and-protection list Fewer than three hazards, or a hazard with no protection or the wrong one. At least three hazards on one machine, each with the right guard, PPE or procedure, and when lockout/tagout is needed. Lists the lockout/tagout steps in order and names the machine's energy sources. Measurement log Limits worked out wrong, or two or more wrong decisions. Limits are correct and at least 4 of 5 practice parts are judged right. All 5 are right, with the measuring habits used written beside the log. Defect record and 5 Whys No separation of bad parts, or the chain stops at the symptom. A check sheet, a step to tag bad parts and a 5 Whys that ends at a fixable cause. Adds a Plan-Do-Check-Act note on how to check that the fix worked. 5S and daily-check plan Missing one of the 5 S's, or fewer than five check items. One action for each S and at least five daily check items with what to report. Names at least two lean wastes in the area and a small improvement for each. CPT 4.0 and job plan Wrong modules, no dates, or a résumé line that claims a credential not earned. Names the four required modules with target dates to confirm, one program or testing site, three job leads and an honest résumé line. Includes a practiced 30-second answer and a backup path such as an apprenticeship. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check again.

check.q: You passed only the Safety module. Which résumé line is honest?
check.why: It names exactly what you earned and does not claim the full CPT 4.0.

check.q: Where do you confirm current CPT fees and testing sites?
options: The official MSSC site or an approved testing site
check.why: Fees and testing change, so check MSSC or the testing site directly.
